exactError: Error: integrate(): Case C reached with candidate 181:3 whose destination would have moved past 180:2 — this disproves Engine Spec §6.2 sub-case iii-d (Test Plan §14.2 MUT-KILL-01).
keyObservation: Firefox (slot 1 in this run) again ends up far ahead of the server and the other two clients (896 vs 761), which agree with each other exactly — identical shape to R0005/R0006/SLOTPERMUTE-iter4. Critically, THIS run used the real, separate delayRelay.ts relay process, not Playwright's routeWebSocket() API at all. This rules out the hypothesis raised after the slot-permutation result: that Firefox's involvement was an artifact of Playwright's own WebSocket-interception fidelity for Firefox specifically (Firefox uses a structurally different remote-control protocol, Juggler, vs Chromium/WebKit's CDP). Firefox is now implicated in 4 of 4 node-dumped failures across two structurally independent injection mechanisms, independent of slot position. This is now treated as CONFIRMED: a real, product-level, Firefox-specific defect (client-side, not server/engine-side, since server + other 2 clients + independent replay all agree with each other every time) — not a testing-tool artifact of either injection mechanism.
reproducibilityCaveat: Same as R0005/R0006 — full node-level ground truth captured (all 3 clients' node counts + server replay's node count), not a byte-exact wire-trace reproducer of this specific trial. This is the strongest entry in the corpus so far for establishing WHICH PARTY is defective (definitively the Firefox client, not the engine/server), even though the exact code path within the Firefox client's own execution is still not identified.
status: SUPERSEDED CONCLUSION, RESOLVED overall — see tests/regression/README.md's FINAL RESOLUTION section, 2026-08-31. This entry's own conclusion ('a real, product-level, Firefox-client-specific defect... CONFIRMED') was premature and has been corrected: a later native-routeWebSocket run froze WebKit's connection instead of Firefox's with the identical signature, showing the defect is not Firefox-exclusive. Send-vs-receive instrumentation plus an 8-run zero-injection direct-path control (0/8 freezes, vs. reproducing within 1-3 attempts under either injection mechanism) traced the actual mechanism to the test harness's delay-injection layer, not to Firefox or any other part of the shipped product. Entry retained per Rule 2, not removed — kept specifically as a documented example of a conclusion that needed correction as more evidence arrived.
